lead: A singly reinforced beam has a ceiling: the concrete compression block cannot grow beyond xu,max, so its moment capacity stops at Mu,lim. When the factored moment exceeds this, or when floor height restricts the beam depth, we add compression steel Asc near the top and extra tension steel Ast2 near the bottom. The pair forms an internal couple that carries the excess moment. This is common in building frames where beam depths are fixed by floor heights.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1, Chapter 2.2, and the Unit 1 stress block.

sections.h3: When and why compression steel is added

blocks.text: A singly reinforced beam reaches its ceiling when the neutral axis depth xu equals xu,max. The concrete compression block cannot take more, so the moment capacity stops at Mu,lim. If the factored moment Mu is larger, or if the depth cannot be increased, steel is placed near the compression face. This is compression steel, area Asc, at effective cover d′. Extra tension steel Ast2 is added at the bottom.

The section is kept at xu = xu,max to use the full concrete capacity. The compression force is C = 0.36 fck b xu + fsc Asc. The tension force is T = 0.87 fy Ast. Here fck is concrete strength, b is width, fy is steel yield strength, and fsc is the stress in compression steel.

blocks.where: Mu is the factored design moment in N·mm; Mu,lim is the limiting moment of the singly reinforced section; fsc is the compressive stress in compression steel in N/mm²; Asc is the compression steel area in mm²; d is effective depth; d′ is effective cover to the centre of compression steel.

blocks.text: The excess moment is ΔM = Mu − Mu,lim. Equilibrium gives Ast2 = Asc fsc/(0.87 fy). The compression steel stress fsc comes from strain compatibility: εsc = 0.0035(xu − d′)/xu. Use fsc = 0.87 fy only when εsc is at least the yield strain of the steel. Otherwise fsc = Es εsc, with Es = 200000 N/mm².
Some syllabi call this compression reinforcement. It is common in building frames where beam depth is fixed by floor height, and in beams that must control deflection.

items: Find Mu,lim = 0.36 fck b xu,max (d − 0.42 xu,max) with xu,max from the steel grade.
If Mu ≤ Mu,lim, design a singly reinforced beam; stop.
If Mu > Mu,lim or depth is restricted, set xu = xu,max.
Compute εsc = 0.0035(xu − d′)/xu and fsc = min(0.87 fy, Es εsc).
Compute Ast2 = Asc fsc/(0.87 fy) and Ast,lim = 0.36 fck b xu/(0.87 fy).
Take Ast = Ast,lim + Ast2; check 0.04 bD limits and minimum steel; select bars.

blocks.text: Compression steel only earns its place if it can yield or carry useful stress. With d′/d around 0.05–0.1, εsc usually exceeds yield and fsc = 0.87 fy. For large d′, fsc falls and Asc rises. IS 456 limits both Asc and Ast to 0.04 bD of the gross section. Tension steel must also meet the minimum area for the beam. If ΔM is very large, a deeper beam or a flanged section may be cheaper than heavy doubly reinforced steel; see Chapter 2.4. Compression steel reduces long-term deflection and cracking, but the beam still needs the serviceability checks of Chapter 2.6.

figure.caption: The steel grade fixes xu,max = 240 mm, which gives Mu,lim; the excess moment ΔM = 34.43 kN·m is then sized as compression steel Asc = 211.93 mm², matched by extra tension steel Ast2 = 211.93 mm².

spec.aria: Flowchart from excess moment to fixing the neutral axis, sizing compression steel, then adding the matching tension steel.

examples.question: Design the compression and tension steel for a rectangular beam with b = 250 mm, d = 500 mm, d′ = 50 mm, fck = 25 N/mm², fy = 415 N/mm², and factored moment Mu = 250 kN·m. Take Mu,lim = 215.57 kN·m.
steps: Mu = 250 kN·m > Mu,lim, so the beam is doubly reinforced. Excess moment ΔM = 250 − 215.57 = 34.43 kN·m = 34.43 × 10<sup>6</sup> N·mm.
Strain in compression steel: εsc = 0.0035 × (240 − 50)/240 = 0.002771. Yield strain for Fe 415 = 0.87 × 415/200000 = 0.001805. Since εsc > yield strain, compression steel yields.
Extra tension steel Ast2 = Asc fsc/(0.87 fy) = 211.93 × 361.05/361.05 = 211.93 mm².
Limiting tension steel Ast,lim = 0.36 fck b xu/(0.87 fy) = 0.36 × 25 × 250 × 240/361.05 = 1495.64 mm².
Total tension steel Ast = Ast,lim + Ast2 = 1495.64 + 211.93 = 1707.56 mm² (using unrounded values).
Provide 4 bars of 25 mm diameter: area = 4 × 491 = 1964 mm² > 1707.56 mm². Provide 2 bars of 16 mm at top: area = 402 mm² > 211.93 mm².
Check 0.04 bD: with overall depth D ≈ 550 mm, 0.04 bD = 0.04 × 250 × 550 = 5500 mm², both steel areas are below the limit.
examples.answer: Asc = 211.93 mm² and Ast = 1707.56 mm²; provide 2–16 mm compression bars and 4–25 mm tension bars.
examples.check:
b = 250
d = 500
dp = 50
fck = 25
fy = 415
Mu = 250e6

xu = 0.48 * d
Mu_lim = 0.36 * fck * b * xu * (d - 0.42 * xu)
delta_M = Mu - Mu_lim
eps_sc = 0.0035 * (xu - dp) / xu
Es = 200000
fsc = min(0.87 * fy, Es * eps_sc)
Asc = delta_M / (fsc * (d - dp))
Ast2 = Asc * fsc / (0.87 * fy)
Ast_lim = 0.36 * fck * b * xu / (0.87 * fy)
Ast = Ast_lim + Ast2

print(f"{Mu_lim/1e6:.2f}")
print(f"{delta_M/1e6:.2f}")
print(f"{xu:.2f}")
print(f"{eps_sc:.6f}")
print(f"{fsc:.2f}")
print(f"{Asc:.2f}")
print(f"{Ast2:.2f}")
print(f"{Ast_lim:.2f}")
print(f"{Ast:.2f}")

traps: Adding Asc but forgetting Ast2: the compression steel force must be balanced by extra tension steel; otherwise the section is not in equilibrium.
Taking fsc = 0.87fy always. For large d′ or small xu, εsc may be below yield; use fsc = Es εsc.
Using total Ast in the concrete block term. The concrete contribution is fixed by xu,max and Ast,lim; the extra steel only carries ΔM.
Unit slip: Mu in kN·m must be converted to N·mm before dividing by fsc(d − d′) in N/mm² and mm.
Setting xu = xu,max when Mu < Mu,lim; this overestimates concrete capacity and gives wrong steel.

quiz.q: What is a doubly reinforced beam?
quiz.a: A beam section with compression steel Asc near the compression face in addition to tension steel Ast near the tension face; the compression steel carries part of the moment when Mu > Mu,lim or when the depth is restricted.

quiz.q: Why is xu set equal to xu,max in the design of a doubly reinforced beam?
quiz.a: To use the full concrete compression capacity Mu,lim; any extra moment is then carried by the steel couple Asc–Ast2, not by increasing the concrete block.

quiz.q: For b = 250 mm, d = 500 mm, d′ = 50 mm, fck = 25 N/mm², fy = 415 N/mm² and Mu = 250 kN·m, find Asc and Ast. Use Mu,lim = 215.57 kN·m.
If d′ is 150 mm in the same beam and xu remains 240 mm, does the compression steel yield? Find fsc and explain the effect on Asc.
quiz.a: εsc = 0.0035(240−150)/240 = 0.0013125. Yield strain of Fe 415 is 0.001805, so εsc is below yield and the compression steel does not yield. Hence fsc = Es εsc = 200000 × 0.0013125 = 262.5 N/mm², not 361.05 N/mm². Asc = ΔM/[fsc(d − d′)] = 34.43 × 10<sup>6</sup>/(262.5 × 350) = 374.8 mm², larger than the 211.93 mm² needed when d′ = 50 mm. A larger d′ lowers the compression steel strain, lowers fsc, and so needs more compression steel for the same excess moment.

quiz.q: Compute Ast,lim for b = 300 mm, d = 550 mm, fck = 30 N/mm², fy = 500 N/mm². Take xu,max/d = 0.46.
Why does compression steel improve beam behaviour at service loads?
quiz.a: It reduces long-term deflection and crack width because it shares compression and restrains creep and shrinkage; the serviceability checks still apply.

quiz.q: What happens if Mu is less than Mu,lim?
quiz.a: A singly reinforced beam is sufficient; adding compression steel is unnecessary and uneconomical. Doubly reinforced design is used only when Mu exceeds Mu,lim or depth is restricted.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, doubly reinforced sections appear in seismic frames where top steel must run through beam-column joints and in retrofits where depth cannot change. Design software solves the same strain-compatibility equations but also checks ductility, bar congestion and fire cover. Higher-grade steel makes the yield strain larger, so compression steel yields less often at a given d′. Search next for strain compatibility design of doubly reinforced sections, compression reinforcement limits in IS 456, and seismic detailing of beam reinforcement.
